# The DPO loss (Eq. 7, page 4)

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\pi_\theta;\pi_{\text{ref}}) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\right)\right]
$$

**Symbols:**
- $y_w$ and $y_l$ are the preferred and dispreferred completions for prompt $x$ (p. 3).
- $\sigma$ is the logistic function (p. 3).
- $\beta$ controls how far the policy may deviate from the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, which is usually the SFT model (p. 4).

The paper presents this as the analogue of the reward-model loss in Eq. 2, $-\mathbb{E}[\log\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l))]$ (pp. 3–4). Its PyTorch version computes the same quantity as `-F.logsigmoid(beta * (pi_logratios - ref_logratios))` (p. 20).

# What plays the role of the reward

The reward is implicit. It is the scaled log-ratio between the policy and the reference model:

$$
\hat r_\theta(x,y) = \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}
$$

The paper calls this "the reward implicitly defined by the language model $\pi_\theta$ and reference model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$" (p. 5). It follows from the steps below.

**Where it comes from.**
- Rearranging the optimal KL-constrained policy gives $r(x,y) = \beta\log\frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta\log Z(x)$ (Eq. 5, p. 4).
- The Bradley-Terry model depends only on reward differences, so the partition function $Z(x)$ cancels (p. 4).
- As a result, the policy network "represents both the language model and the (implicit) reward" (p. 4). DPO thereby "fit[s] an implicit reward using an alternative parameterization, whose optimal policy is simply $\pi_\theta$" (p. 4).

**Why this costs no generality.** Theorem 1 states that, under mild assumptions, every reward class consistent with Plackett-Luce/Bradley-Terry can be represented as $\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ for some model $\pi$ (p. 6). This is the sense of the section title "Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model" (p. 5).

**How it appears in training.**
- In the gradient, each example is weighted by $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$. That weight is higher when the implicit reward orders the pair incorrectly (p. 5).
- The reference code returns `rewards = beta * (pi_logps - ref_logps).detach()` (p. 20).

# A note on sign

Appendix A.4, Eq. 21 (p. 17), writes the argument of $\log\sigma$ with the $y_l$ and $y_w$ terms swapped relative to Eq. 7. The main-text Eq. 7 (p. 4), the A.2 derivation (p. 16), and the code (p. 20) all use the "preferred minus dispreferred" form shown above.
